t: Feminism holds that modern societies are patriarchal, and since the late 18th century its movements have campaigned for women’s right to vote, hold office, work, earn equal pay, own property and receive education.

Its Western history is told in waves: suffrage movements in the 19th and early 20th centuries, the women’s liberation movement from the 1960s, a third wave from about 1992 and a fourth, of social media, from about 2012.

Liberal, socialist and radical feminism, the “Big Three”, have been joined by Black, postcolonial, intersectional and other feminisms, born largely of the criticism that the movement spoke for white, middle-class women.
dyk: The word began as a term of disapproval: “féminisme” first appeared in an 1871 French medical thesis on men with tuberculosis who had developed feminine traits, and in 1872 Alexandre Dumas fils coined “féministe” for men who supported women’s rights.
ev: Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, arguing that women as much as men need equal rights
The self-governing colony of New Zealand grants women the right to vote
The Representation of the People Act gives the vote to British women over 30 who own property
The Nineteenth Amendment grants American women the vote in all states, closing the first wave in the United States
Simone de Beauvoir publishes The Second Sex
Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique sparks the beginning of second-wave feminism in the United States
Rebecca Walker’s article “Becoming the Third Wave” gives the third wave its name
Time names activists of the #MeToo movement, “the silence breakers”, its Person of the Year

f.thinkers: Mary Wollstonecraft, seen by many as its founder; John Stuart Mill, of the liberal tradition; Clara Zetkin, leader of the German social-democratic women’s movement; Simone de Beauvoir, existentialist author of The Second Sex; Betty Friedan, whose book sparked the American second wave; bell hooks and Audre Lorde, who made room for race in feminist thought; Catharine MacKinnon, radical feminist
f.texts: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792); Qasim Amin, The Liberation of Women (1899); Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own (1929); Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949); Betty Friedan, The Feminine Mystique (1963); Germaine Greer, The Female Eunuch (1970); Rebecca Walker, “Becoming the Third Wave” (1992)
f.ideas: modern societies are patriarchal and treat women unjustly; equal political, legal and economic rights for women; “the personal is political”; gender roles as socially constructed rather than fixed by biology; women’s right to control their own bodies and sexuality; intersectionality, the joining of sex with race, class and other inequalities
f.today: a family of schools, liberal, radical, socialist and Marxist, Black, postcolonial and intersectional among them; a fourth wave since about 2012, working through social media and best known for the #MeToo movement; defined by UN Women in 2024 and by 28 Nordic feminist bodies in 2025 as a movement grounded in human rights and intersectionality
